p5.intro: p5.js is a free JavaScript library for drawing, animating and responding to input in a web page. It grew out of Processing, the 'sketchbook' language made for artists, and it is the most used library on Art Blocks. You write a short program, give it a random seed, and every seed draws a different work.

history.text: Casey Reas and Ben Fry start Processing at the MIT Media Lab, a programming language meant for visual artists.
Lauren Lee McCarthy creates p5.js, bringing Processing's ideas to JavaScript and the browser.

get_started: Open the p5.js web editor (editor.p5js.org) and run the default sketch; no install needed.
Follow the first Coding Train p5.js videos: shapes, colour, variables, loops.
Replace Math.random with a seeded random number generator so one seed always draws the same picture.
Read Art Blocks' 'building your project' page to see how tokenData.hash becomes your seed.
Make 20 outputs from 20 seeds and print them on one sheet; keep the rules that surprise you.
p5.starter_cost: Free: p5.js is free and open-source software [sourced: p5js.org]. A laptop you already own is enough.
humanity: The hand: scan one of your own pencil lines and let the code draw with its wobble instead of a perfect curve.
Imperfection: add a small, seeded tremble to every stroke, so no two outputs share the same 'steadiness'.
Collaboration: invite someone who has never coded to choose the rules while you type, and credit them on the token.
Time: let a sketch slowly erase and redraw itself, the way a drawing on a chalkboard fades between classes.

learn_links.label: Art Blocks: building your project (tokenData, PRNG)

p5.first_project: Draw 100 random lines from one seed; change the seed and see a new output. That is long-form generative art in miniature.

glsl.intro: Shaders are small programs that run on the graphics card and decide the colour of every pixel at once. GLSL is the language they are written in, and WebGL is how browsers run them. They make dense, fast, glowing images and are behind about a third of Art Blocks projects in our data.

history.text: GLSL becomes part of core OpenGL with OpenGL 2.0, making programmable shading standard on graphics cards.
WebGL 1.0 is released, bringing GPU shaders into the web browser.

get_started: Work through the first chapters of The Book of Shaders in its live editor.
Write a fragment shader that colours the screen by x and y, then add time.
Add a noise function and map its value to a two-colour palette.
Pass a seed from JavaScript as a uniform so each token gets its own field.
Check your shader on a phone: precision and speed differ by device.
glsl.starter_cost: Free: browsers include WebGL; The Book of Shaders is free to read online [sourced: thebookofshaders.com].
humanity: Imperfection: GPUs make perfect gradients; add grain, dust and uneven edges so the image feels made, not rendered.
Memory: sample the colours of a photo you care about and let the shader build its palette from them.
The body: drive one uniform from slow breathing (a 4-second in, 6-second out cycle) so the image breathes with a person.
Place: use the sky colour at a real location and hour as the base of the palette.
glsl.first_project: Write a fragment shader that maps a noise field to a two-colour palette, then feed it a seed.

three.intro: three.js is the standard JavaScript library for 3D in the browser: scenes, cameras, lights, materials and meshes. It hides most of WebGL's detail so you can build and orbit a 3D world in a few dozen lines.

history.text: Ricardo Cabello (mrdoob) first releases three.js on GitHub.

get_started: Follow the three.js manual's 'Creating a scene' page and get a spinning cube.
Replace the cube with a seeded grid of boxes whose heights come from the token hash.
Add one light and one material change; keep the scene simple.
Export a frame as PNG and the geometry as .obj (three.js has an OBJ exporter) to test physical output later.
three.starter_cost: Free: three.js is open-source under the MIT license [sourced: github.com/mrdoob/three.js].
humanity: Place: model a room you know by memory, not by measurement, and let the seed rearrange it.
The body: set the camera at the eye height of a real person you name in the work.
Care: light a scene the way you would light a room for someone you love, warm and low, instead of studio-bright.
Making: export the geometry and 3D-print one output, as Aranda\Lasch did with Primitives' .obj files.
three.first_project: Generate a field of boxes whose heights come from a seed; orbit around it.

vanilla.intro: Vanilla JavaScript means plain browser code with no library. On Art Blocks it usually draws to the canvas 2D API directly, which keeps scripts small (they are stored on-chain) and gives full control.

history.text: Apple introduces the canvas element in WebKit; it later becomes part of the HTML standard.

get_started: Read MDN's Canvas tutorial up to 'Drawing shapes' and 'Applying styles and colors'.
Rebuild a small p5 sketch with plain canvas calls and compare file sizes.
Write your own tiny seeded random function (Art Blocks' docs show one).
Handle window resizing yourself so every output scales cleanly.
humanity: The hand: write the drawing loop to move like a pen: start, press, lift, never jump.
Imperfection: keep one deliberate 'mistake' rule, like a line that overshoots its corner.
Time: let the piece draw itself slowly on load so the viewer watches it being made.
vanilla.first_project: Port a small p5 sketch to plain canvas 2D calls; compare file size.

svg.intro: SVG is a vector format: shapes stored as paths and coordinates rather than pixels. Scripts that output SVG can be sent straight to pen plotters, laser cutters and embroidery software, which makes SVG the bridge from code to physical work.

history.text: SVG 1.0 becomes a W3C Recommendation.

get_started: Read MDN's 'SVG from scratch' and hand-write one file with a path.
Generate the same path from a seed in JavaScript and add it to the page.
Add a key press that downloads the current SVG.
Open it in vpype or Inkscape and check line order and duplicate lines before plotting.
svg.starter_cost: Free: SVG is an open web standard; Inkscape and vpype are free software [estimate: no paid tools needed].
humanity: The hand: send the SVG to a plotter with a real pen, so ink bleed and paper texture finish the work.
Collaboration: give the file to an embroiderer, a woodworker or a sign painter and let their craft interpret it.
Imperfection: keep stroke order visible, so the viewer can see how the line was made.
svg.first_project: Render your sketch as SVG paths and open the file in a plotter or vector tool.

interactive.intro: Interactive works respond to the viewer's mouse, touch or keys: a click, a drag, a key press. On Art Blocks this ranges from Chromie Squiggle's simple click-to-animate to works you can play with.

history.text: Some of the earliest interactive art dates to the 1920s, such as Marcel Duchamp's Rotary Glass Plates, which the viewer had to switch on.

get_started: Add one click handler that changes a single layer, while the token hash fixes the rest.
Add keyboard shortcuts and list them in the token description.
Test touch on a phone and a tablet.
Make sure the work still looks finished if nobody touches it.
humanity: The hand: let a long press leave a mark that stays, so each owner's touch becomes part of the piece.
Care: design the interaction to reward patience, like slowly revealing detail only after someone stays.
Collaboration: let two people's clicks combine, so the work needs more than one hand.
Memory: keep the last interaction in local storage, so the piece remembers its last visitor on that device.
interactive.first_project: Let a click reseed one layer of the piece while the token hash fixes the rest.

clock.intro: Clock-driven works read the time and change with it: by hour, day or season. Alexis André's 720 Minutes, which changes through the day, is an early Art Blocks example.
get_started: Read the hour with new Date() and map it to a palette.
Check the piece at noon and midnight, and in another time zone.
Decide whether to use the viewer's local time or one fixed place's time, and say which in the description.
Add a test mode that fakes the clock so you can preview all states.
humanity: Time: make a piece that is only complete when watched across a whole day.
Place: fix the clock to the time zone of a place that matters to you, so viewers elsewhere see 'your' hour.
Memory: mark an anniversary date with a one-day-only state.
The body: follow sunrise and sunset, which shift through the year, instead of the clock's even hours.
clock.first_project: Shift the palette with the hour of day; check it at noon and midnight.

fetch.intro: Some Art Blocks scripts fetch live data from the web when they render, so the work can change with the world. It is powerful but fragile: if the source goes away, the work must still render.

history.text: Jesse James Garrett's article (Feb 18, 2005) coins the term Ajax for web pages that fetch data in the background.

get_started: Fetch one public value (for example the latest block number) and let it nudge one parameter.
Always include a fallback render when offline.
Cache nothing private; never send viewer data anywhere.
Write in the description what is fetched and from where.
fetch.starter_cost: Free for public APIs; some data providers charge [estimate].
humanity: Place: read the weather of one town and let it set the mood of the piece.
Care: tie the work to a public good (a river level, an air reading) so watching it means watching over something.
Memory: if the source disappears, freeze the last state as a record of when it stopped.
fetch.first_project: Fetch one public value (for example a block number) and let it nudge a parameter; render a fallback when offline.

Process everything on the device; store nothing.
cv.starter_cost: Free; a webcam you already own.
humanity: The body: let the viewer's posture shape the work.
Collaboration: draw together with the camera, as Sougwen Chung does with her robots.
Care: process images locally and say so plainly.
Imperfection: keep jitter from the camera rather than smoothing it away.
cv.first_project: Use the webcam image as a mask for a generative pattern.

bio.intro: Works shaped by body data such as heartbeat. Beervangeer & Studio Poca's Totem: Symbols of Change (2023) is the Art Blocks example in our maturity map.
get_started: Pair a Bluetooth heart-rate strap with Web Bluetooth (Chrome) on a laptop.
Capture one reading at a chosen moment and use it as a seed.
Store nothing else; say so in the description.
bio.starter_cost: A Bluetooth chest strap costs tens of dollars [estimate].
humanity: The body: the heartbeat at the moment of minting becomes the work's pulse.
Care: ask consent clearly and keep body data private.
Memory: capture a heartbeat at a moment that matters (a first meeting, a goodbye).
bio.first_project: Capture heart rate once at mint from a Bluetooth chest strap and use it as a seed (capture once, store nothing else).

eeg.intro: Brain-signal input from consumer EEG headsets, smoothed into slow changes in the work.

history.text: Hans Berger records the first human EEG.

get_started: Read the OpenBCI getting-started docs.
Stream one signal into a sketch and smooth it heavily.
Treat it as mood, not mind-reading.
eeg.starter_cost: Consumer EEG boards cost hundreds of dollars [estimate].
humanity: The body: let stillness, not effort, make the strongest image.
Care: be honest that the signal is noisy and personal.
Collaboration: two people wearing sensors shape one image.
eeg.first_project: Stream an OpenBCI signal into a sketch and smooth it heavily.

env.intro: Air quality, temperature or weather read by a local sensor, so the work reflects the room or city it is in.
get_started: Follow Adafruit's PM2.5 sensor guide with a microcontroller.
Send the reading to a running token view.
Map it to one parameter, like density.
env.starter_cost: A PM2.5 sensor and microcontroller cost tens of dollars [estimate].
humanity: Place: the work only makes sense where it is installed.
Care: make the air visible so people notice it.
Time: let a year of readings build one image.

learn_links.label: Adafruit: PM2.5 air quality sensor guide

env.first_project: Wire a PM2.5 sensor to a microcontroller and let the reading change density in a running token view.

motion.intro: Phone tilt and motion as input, read with the browser's device orientation events.
get_started: Read MDN's 'Detecting device orientation'.
Ask permission on iOS with a button.
Tilt to rotate the composition.
humanity: The body: the work moves only when the viewer moves.
Imperfection: keep hand shake as texture.
Place: let walking change the piece.
motion.first_project: Tilt the phone to rotate the composition.

haptics.intro: Vibration as output on phones, through the Vibration API (supported on Android browsers; not on iPhone Safari).
get_started: Read MDN's Vibration API page.
Pulse the phone in a seeded rhythm.

humanity: The body: a rhythm felt in the hand, like a pulse.
Care: make it gentle and easy to turn off.
Memory: encode a remembered rhythm (a knock, a song).
haptics.first_project: Pulse the phone in a seeded rhythm.

gps.intro: Location as input or as a condition to mint. Harvey Rayner's marfaMESH (2023) used location clusters in Marfa, Texas.

history.text: GPS becomes fully operational.

get_started: Read MDN's Geolocation API page.
Use coarse location only, with consent.
Change one parameter by city or region, never store coordinates.
humanity: Place: a work that can only be minted where it was made.
Memory: tie each output to a place you walked.
Care: never store exact locations.
gps.first_project: Change the palette by city (coarse location only, with consent).

get_started: Open an A-Frame or three.js WebXR example on a laptop.
Open the same page in a headset browser.
Add a seeded scene.
Keep frame rate high; test seated and standing.
xr.starter_cost: A used standalone headset costs a few hundred dollars [estimate].
humanity: The body: scale everything to a real human body.
Place: rebuild a place from memory.
Care: give the viewer a calm, safe place to stand.
Collaboration: make a space two people can share.
xr.first_project: Load a three.js piece in WebXR and walk around it.

mr.intro: Mixed-reality headsets like Apple Vision Pro, which blend digital objects with the real room.

history.text: Apple Vision Pro goes on sale in the US on February 2, 2024.

get_started: Open a WebXR scene in the headset's browser.
Place one seeded object on a real table.
Keep it small and still.
humanity: Place: the work lives in your actual room.
The body: let it react to the viewer's distance.
Care: keep the real room visible.
mr.first_project: Open a WebXR version of your piece in the headset browser before building a native app.

glasses.intro: Smart glasses that show small displays over the world. No token-linked art found yet.

history.text: Google Glass is in early use through its Explorer program.

get_started: Read the platform's developer docs.
Show one small, quiet element.
Test outdoors.
humanity: Place: a work seen only on a walk.
Care: keep it quiet and glanceable.
Time: show it only at dusk.

history.text: Clément Ader demonstrates stereo telephone listening (the théâtrophone) in Paris, an early form of binaural sound.

get_started: Use Web Audio's PannerNode to place a sound.
Move it slowly around the listener.
Test on headphones.
humanity: The body: sound that circles the head like breath.
Place: record a real place binaurally and let the seed recompose it.
Care: make something for one person, alone, with headphones.
spatial.first_project: Pan three seeded voices around the listener with a PannerNode.

holo.intro: Holographic, volumetric and stereoscopic displays show depth without a headset. A.A. Murakami's Floating World Genesis and the 2021 Looking Glass × Reggie Watts hologram are examples in our map.

history.text: Dennis Gabor invents holography (Nobel Prize 1971).

get_started: Read the Looking Glass developer docs.
Render a seeded three.js scene as a quilt of views.
Show it on a display or as a light-field print.
holo.starter_cost: Light-field displays cost hundreds of dollars or more [estimate].
humanity: The body: depth that changes as you move your head.
Memory: a remembered object floating in space.
Care: make a quiet object, not a spectacle.
holo.first_project: Export a three.js scene to a light-field display.

plotter.intro: A pen plotter is a machine that draws with a real pen, following vector paths. It is the 'house' physical format of on-chain generative art: Tyler Hobbs's Fidenza (2021) and Licia He's Running Moon are verified plotter works in our data, and Plottables is a platform built for it.

history.text: Georg Nees and others show some of the first computer drawings made on plotters.
Earliest first mint on the Plottables contract (plotter-first generative art on Art Blocks technology) in our data: Streamlines by NumbersInMotion.

get_started: Make your sketch output SVG paths.
Clean the SVG with vpype: merge lines, sort for travel, remove duplicates.
Plot on a borrowed or hobby plotter (AxiDraw or similar) with one pen.
Try three papers and two pens; keep notes.
Decide how a token holder gets a plot, and record it.
plotter.starter_cost: A hobby plotter costs a few hundred dollars; makerspaces often have one [estimate].
humanity: The hand: let pen pressure, ink bleed and paper tooth finish what the code started.
Imperfection: Licia He makes plotter paintings and calls her plotters robots (per her site); let paint skip and pool.
Time: a plot can take hours; film it and share the slowness.
Care: sign and date each plot by hand.
plotter.first_project: Export one SVG from your sketch, optimise it with vpype and plot it on A4.

prints.intro: Inkjet, giclée and archival prints turn the screen image into a physical object on paper. Many Art Blocks artists (Fidenza, Meridian, Ringers, Chromie Squiggle) offer or authorise prints.

history.text: The term giclée is coined for fine-art inkjet prints.

get_started: Render a very high-resolution output (for example 8,000+ pixels on the long side).
Order one proof from a print lab on two papers.
Compare colour; adjust and reprint.
Decide edition size and how it links to the token (a QR code or NFC tag on the back).
prints.starter_cost: A single fine-art proof costs tens of dollars [estimate].
humanity: The hand: sign each print and write the token number by hand.
Care: pick paper that will outlive you.
Collaboration: work with one printer you trust and credit them.
Memory: keep the first proof, with its mistakes, as part of the story.
prints.first_project: Render your token at print resolution (set pixelDensity, then saveCanvas) and proof it at a local print shop.

screen.intro: Screen printing pushes ink through a stencil on mesh, one colour at a time. Dmitri Cherniak's Ringers #962: The LACMA Iterations (2023) is a screen-printed series from a single token.

history.text: Andy Warhol and others make screen printing a major art medium.

get_started: Split your output into 2–4 flat colours.
Export one SVG or high-contrast PNG per colour.
Book time at a print studio or makerspace.
Print a small run and register each layer by hand.
screen.starter_cost: A community studio session costs tens of dollars [estimate].
humanity: The hand: every pull of the squeegee is slightly different; keep the differences.
Imperfection: misregistration is part of the look.
Collaboration: print with a master printer and credit them.
Memory: number each print and keep a record of which screen made it.
screen.first_project: Separate your output into 2 colour layers and print a test with a local studio.

riso.intro: Risograph is a stencil-based printer that prints in bright soy inks, one colour at a time, with a grainy, imperfect look. Pandelune's Reverie (2024) is the Art Blocks example in our map.

history.text: Riso Kagaku Corporation introduces the Risograph in Japan.

get_started: Split your output into 2–3 colours.
Export one grayscale file per colour.
Book a riso studio (many cities have one).
Print a small zine of outputs.
riso.starter_cost: A riso studio run costs tens of dollars [estimate].
humanity: Imperfection: riso grain and offset are the point.
Collaboration: make a zine with friends, one page each.
Memory: print a small run and give it away by hand.
riso.first_project: Export each colour as its own greyscale layer and run 10 different outputs.

darkroom.intro: Darkroom, film and cyanotype processes make images with light and chemistry. Dmitri Cherniak's Light Years (2022) and Trevor Paglen's PRELUDES connect this tradition to tokens.

history.text: John Herschel discovers the cyanotype process.
Anna Atkins publishes Photographs of British Algae: Cyanotype Impressions, often called the first book illustrated with photographs.

get_started: Print your output as a transparency (an inkjet negative).
Coat paper with cyanotype chemistry (kits are sold online).
Expose in sunlight, rinse in water.
Scan the result and compare to the screen.
darkroom.starter_cost: A cyanotype kit costs under fifty dollars [estimate].
humanity: Time: sunlight sets the exposure; the day's weather becomes part of the work.
The hand: brush marks from coating stay on the paper.
Place: expose under the sun of a place that matters to you.
Imperfection: no two prints match; that is the edition.
darkroom.first_project: Print your output as a transparency and make a cyanotype in sunlight.

Convert it to a stitch file with Ink/Stitch (free Inkscape extension).
Stitch one test on a home embroidery machine or at a makerspace.
Adjust density and stitch type; stitch again.
embroid.starter_cost: A home embroidery machine costs a few hundred dollars [estimate].
humanity: The hand: finish a machine-stitched piece with a few hand stitches.
Care: stitch something to be worn or used, not just framed.
Memory: embroider on fabric that belonged to someone.
Collaboration: send the file to an embroiderer and credit them.
embroid.first_project: Turn one SVG output into a stitch file with Ink/Stitch and sew a 10 cm patch.

weave.intro: Weaving, Jacquard looms, tapestry and cane all build images from crossing threads. The Jacquard loom's punched cards inspired early computing; today Alexis André's Navette and Aranda\Lasch's Enlace bring weaving to tokens.

history.text: Joseph Marie Jacquard demonstrates his punched-card loom.

get_started: Reduce your output to a grid of a few thread colours.
Export the grid as a bitmap.
Ask a Jacquard studio (like TRAME, Navette's partner) for their file spec.
Weave a small sample first.
weave.starter_cost: Studio Jacquard sampling costs vary widely [estimate].
humanity: The hand: weavers make choices the file cannot; ask them to.
Time: a loom shows how long things take.
Memory: weave with yarn from an old garment.
Collaboration: credit the weaver alongside the code.
weave.first_project: Quantise your output to 6 colours and a thread grid; ask a weaving studio for a sample quote.

knit.intro: Knitting machines turn a pixel grid into fabric, stitch by stitch. A.A. Murakami × TRAME's ASARI and Licia He's Yarntificial City are examples in our map.

Find a hackable or industrial knitting service.
Knit a swatch.
Adjust for stretch: stitches are not square.
knit.starter_cost: Used domestic knitting machines can cost a few hundred dollars [estimate].
humanity: The body: fabric meant to be worn takes the shape of a person.
Care: knit something for someone.
Imperfection: dropped stitches show the machine is human-tended.

fashion.intro: Generative fashion and apparel put the work on bodies: tees, dresses, scarves. 9dcc × Snowfro's ITERATION-02 (2022) and Nathan Cornes's Generative Couture are examples.

Order a print-on-demand sample.
Try it on and photograph it in daylight.
Decide how the garment links to the token (an NFC tag).
fashion.starter_cost: Print-on-demand samples cost tens of dollars [estimate].
humanity: The body: the work moves with a person.

Turn output into that method's file (grid or stitches).
Make one physical sample.
Photograph it next to the screen version.

Collaboration: work with a maker and credit them.

laser.intro: Laser cutters cut or engrave wood, paper, acrylic and fabric from vector files. Shawn Kemp's fx(mandala) (2022, fxhash) is the example in our map.

Book a makerspace laser.
Cut in cardboard first, then the real material.

Generate toolpaths in CAM software.
Mill in foam or soft wood first.

Send it to a foundry or a casting service.

Translate one output into a glaze or carved pattern.
Fire and photograph it.

humanity: The hand: clay records every touch.
Imperfection: kiln results are never certain.
Care: make something to eat from.

Work with a stained-glass studio.
